raw_segments.text: The poet is speaking in his own person. He never leads us to suppose that he is anyone else. But in what follows he takes the person of Chryses, and then he does all that he can to make us believe that the speaker is not Homer, but the aged priest himself.
And in this double form he has cast the entire narrative of the events which occurred at Troy and in Ithaca and throughout the Odyssey.
The poet is speaking in his own person. He never leads us to suppose that he is anyone else.
But in what follows, he takes the person of Chryses, and then he does all that he can to make us believe that the speaker is not Homer, but the aged priest himself.
And in this double form, he has cast the entire narrative of the events which occurred at Troy, and in Ithaca, and throughout the Odyssey.
